newsitem.title: JAPAN: High Japan oil product stocks could limit imports.
newsitem.headline: High Japan oil product stocks could limit imports.

text.p: A major surge in Japan's petroleum product inventories, highlighted on Monday by statistics from the country's Trade Ministry, is likely to diminish Japan's presence in regional product markets this summer, traders said.

Japan's end-April product stocks as a whole were up some 22.8 percent from a year earlier, at 14.52 million kilolitres (kl) or 91,356 barrels, according to statistics released on Monday by the Ministry of International Trade and Industry (MITI).
Inventories of kerosene, Japan's most important home-heating fuel, rose dramatically by 50.5 percent year-on-year in April to 2.74 million kl (17.23 million barrels).
Gas oil stocks stood at 2.45 million kl (15.41 million barrels), up 24.4 percent from a year earlier.

Traders say the builds are attributable to a warmer than normal winter following a period in which Japan's refiners had stepped up kerosene imports and production in order to match stock levels seen during the 1995/96 winter.
Japan's April weather continued that trend, with temperatures some 1.2 degrees centigrade warmer than during the same month a year earlier, MITI officials said.

Traders say the resulting high stocks probably influenced operational planning by Japan's oil refinery executives, who in May were required by MITI to submit annual production and import projections for this fiscal year.
Industry sources say that imports, rather than refinery operating rates, will likely suffer first from the high stocks.
"The first step traditionally is to cut imports. This is usually done before production is reduced," a trader with a major oil firm said.
Imports of kerosene in June 1996 were 127,000 kl, while imports of gas oil were 241,000 kl.
Together, that amounts to 77,000 bpd of kerosene and gas oil demand in regional markets, a figure likely to decline this June in light of the high stock levels.
Japan typically imports products from Singapore markets, through Middle East term contracts, and from South Korean refiners.
Traders say that the country's peak period of refinery maintenance during May and June could provide some relief, with lower-than-normal production levels leading to stock drawdowns.
